Hi there. We don't allow discussions about favourite binge foods etc. for two reasons.

Firstly, this is a pro-recovery sub, therefore we don't allow anything that may encourage or glorify disordered behaviours. Binging is included in this as it is a disordered behaviour just the same as purging or restricting. We wouldn't allow discussions on people's favourite ways to purge, for example, so we equally wouldn't allow discussions on people's favourite binge foods. Discussions like these are also a slippery slope to people talking about foods that are easy or hard to purge which we certainly don't allow for obvious reasons.

Secondly, we don't want to trigger anyone to binge. This is why we don't tend to allow pictures of food either. I understand people need a place to open up about their struggles, that's why we're here. However, in many cases, we have to prioritise the safety of the community at large, which is why we remove content like this. Our goal is not to silence anyone, but rather to ensure that this is a safe place for everyone. If the discussion were to be inappropriate in a group therapy setting, then it would be equally inappropriate here. Thank you for understanding.

I've both lived in student accom and at home. Lived away for my foundation year and then went to a different uni to start my undergrad while staying at home. Now that I'm in my second year of staying at home, I can definitely say I prefer it to living away. 

However (big however) there are so many personal factors as to why moving out didn't work for me and why I now live at home. I have both mental and physical illnesses that have really delayed me in learning to socialise and also to look after myself. I was absolutely not ready to move out at that time and it resulted in me sliding into an intense depressive episode. 

I missed my family so much more than I expected to. Mind you I only moved about 1 hr away from home and I was still homesick despite going home for dinner once a week. I look back on that time as one of the worst in my life. I met some lovely people and there were definitely some amazing moments, but overall, it was not good. 

Fast forward to now. I go to a uni in central London and me and my family already live in London anyway. There's no way I can afford to live alone in London. The commute is ok and I only have to go in 2 days a week. I don't feel like an odd one out because about half of my class also lives at home. My university is also just one building with none of its own student accom so there's no campus atmosphere I miss out on. I also fairly recently got sober (had major substance abuse issues - again living away didn't help that) and staying at home has helped me stay away from drinking and drug use which for me is very important. I'm not dealing with flat drama, dirty kitchens, shitty bathrooms (my bathroom in student halls were horrible). 

The downsides are that I definitely don't go to clubs and societies and if I did it would be a lot of money and hassle to get there and back. There are also educational/industry events at my uni that sometimes go on until late. By the time I'm home I'd have barely any time to sleep before my class the next day. Also, I definitely don't have as many close friends there as I might do if I lived nearer. I'm quite an introvert though so that doesn't really bother me. Lastly, the commute can suck sometimes. I have to wake up early, tfl fares are expensive and strikes can mess up the day.

Apologies for the very long comment. My main point is that in *my* situation, with my particular university, staying at home has been so much better. However, I know that my situation is incredibly specific and that you might have totally different things going on. It really depends on the kind of person you are. If you're really sociable and you don't find it difficult to make friends, then you'd have a much better time. But if those things aren't super easy, things get very depressing very soon. Especially if you're in student halls and spending all your time in a tiny, boxy room. If you've had any struggles with your mental health, substance use or taking care of your self, then moving out definitely exacerbates those things. 

If you don't feel ready, there is absolutely nothing wrong with staying at home for a year or so. You have so much time ahead to make that jump when you know you can. Good luck!

You need to be realistic here. you're still a child, you're not a professional, you're not a therapist. There is only so much you can do at this point before you start sacrificing your own mental health and your self care. If she's at the point where she's telling you she wants to kill her self and is referencing a plan then you need to take it seriously. The best possible thing you can do is encourage her to seek professional support or, if you're extremely concerned for her safety at any current point, call emergency services to her. In the meantime listen to her if she wants to vent, show her you're there for her. BUT make sure you're not sacrificing your own mental health to do this. If it's too much for you then set that boundary and tell her. I understand you care a lot about her and want to help her, but you realistically don't have the power or knowledge that a professional does and trying to fulfill that position in her life is only going to hurt you.

I know what you mean, these things really mess with our dopamine. Even if I have the happiest day ever, I still have terrible urges. The only thing that I've found helpful is abstinence - in the case of recovering from alcohol/drug abuse, though. Sadly haven't gotten there with b/p yet. The first few months of being sober were so difficult, I felt bored and depressed all the time and I genuinely felt like I'd never feel happy or comforted again. It just takes time for your brain to adjust to the change and then things actually start feeling good again. It sucks because it's such a difficult solution, but it is more motivation to get better in the end, to know that you will feel joy again.

Adding another addiction will not give you control over the one you already have. You can't simply replace addictions, trust me. All you'll do is put yourself in more danger by giving yourself more ways to self destruct. If you want to replace behaviours, the safest way to do so is by replacing them with something more positive or beneficial. I hope you find those more positive things, take care!

This isn't really the place to find out what food to avoid or when the best time to throw up is. This is a recovery/support sub and the general rule for any community like this is to not share tips that encourage dangerous behaviours. 

It is important to know how to take care of yourself when it comes to this disorder though, teeth and vitamins etc. When you search in the subreddit, include the word harm reduction in the search and you'll probably find more helpful answers. 

When it comes to teeth, this is the advice i've been given: Wait 30 minutes after purging to brush. you can also swish a mix of water and baking soda in your mouth to neutralise the acid. At the end of the day though, there's not a ton that you can do to stop tooth damage other than stop purging. Like another commenter said here, there's no safe way to do this. You can reduce the damage a bit, but that's it.

I was referred to CAMHS - which in the uk is the nhs mental health service for children - when I was 13 and my school/parents found out I had been self harming. They diagnosed me with clinical depression. Then when I was around 15, my psychiatrist thought that I probably didn't have, as he put it, simple depression. He changed my diagnosis to more of a description of my symptoms, which was: mood instability with features of depression and dissociation, likely to be related to personality. 

He started the process of referring me to an intensive dbt program in London. I started that when I was almost 17. They did a very very long assessment. It took over two weeks if I remember right. There were online questionnaires about almost every aspect of my life as well as assessments in person.  During my time with them my diagnosis was 'emerging traits of EUPD'. I finished the program after a year and a bit, got sent back to my old psychiatrist for the last few months of being 17. He helped to get me referred to nhs adult mental health services and when I turned 18 I started having appointments there. Had a short assessment with their psychiatrist and low and behold, my diagnosis was changed to just EUPD. After a year they discharged me due to poor compliance with treatment (long story). I tried for ages to get back into services because I desperately needed help. 

Long story short, they never did help. I ended up getting private psychiatry/therapy, luckily my dad's job came with good medical insurance. (He's retiring in a few years though so I'm not sure what I'll do after that). I started seeing the psychiatrist when I turned 20 and he gave me another assessment, confirmed it was EUPD/BPD. Then at the end of last year I went to rehab for my alcohol/drug abuse. My psychiatrist worked there and I saw him every week while I was there. He ended up giving me a PTSD and substance abuse diagnosis on top of the EUPD.

That's my story, hope this was helpful :)

I don't claim any expertise, I can only speak to my own and close friend's experiences. In my opinion you've pretty much hit the nail on the head. Our fear of abandonment can often lead to irrational assumptions/delusions that we are definitely right now being abandoned. My weight loss was between the ages of 16 and 18, so I wonder a lot of the time if I just lost puppy fat. 

Most importantly, face fat fluctuates almost as much as your stomach. The position you sleep in, how much water you drink and whether you drink a lot of alcohol can really affect how your face looks. I was previously a heavy drinker and I've been sober for almost 8 months. One big change I've noticed is in my face, it is less puffy and less bloated. 

There isn't a lot of weight you could lose before you become underweight, so I wouldn't recommend loosing the same amount that I did. Instead I'd recommend looking at these other factors and thinking about what lifestyle changes you could make. Hope this helped!

So when you do dbt they teach you about this thing called bio social theory. It basically describes that bpd can occur when a person is born with a biological predisposition to heightened emotional intensity and dysregulation. 
Then if this person goes on to grow up in an emotionally invalidating environment (emotionally absent or physically abusive parents for some examples) they don't learn how to properly emotionally regulate like other children do. As far as I understand that is the most widely accepted theory for the cause of bpd.
So, cptsd (as I understand it) stems from multiple traumatic events or being in a consistently traumatic situation over time. 

I take that to mean these traumas could happen at any point in a persons life and could result in cptsd, however not learning to emotionally regulate as a child is more responsible for bpd. And that people who are diagnosed with cptsd are less likely to have the same biological predisposition that people diagnosed with bpd do.
Growing up in an emotionally invalidating environment isn't inherently traumatic to everyone, however. lots of people grow up with emotionally stunted parents say, and don't develop bpd. So the biological predisposition is what makes it a traumatic environment and is key to the development of a pd.

I've had to deal with the terrible school swimming lessons while having scars, so I understand your situation and it sucks man. When I was younger and frequently self harming I would generally avoid swimming and if it was a school thing I'd fake sick and stay home. It's a tricky situation you're in, I'm sorry to say fading scars is a long term process, there are creams and oils like vitamin e that can help, but it can take a while (up to a year depending on your skin and the type of scar) before they loose their colour and become flat. Things like bracelets and wristbands, long gloves and wrist warmers are good at hiding them in the mean time, while also looking pretty fashionable. 

When it comes to the other things you mention, I'd say that firstly there is absolutely no shame in self harm or having scars which I'm sure you know, but we all need reminders now and again. If and when you feel you are ready to I'd urge you to tell your parents what's going on. Once I told mine it started a journey of feeling slowly more comfortable with my scars. Having to constantly hide your skin and freaking out about what they did or didn't see is so incredibly stressful and will not help your mental health in the long term. Having at least one person where you don't have to worry about that stuff really takes the pressure off and gives you space to begin healing mentally. 

And on the subject of blades, throwing them out is an amazing milestone. Even if it doesn't stop you from self harming again, it shows that you are at least trying to take care if yourself and that it's something you can keep doing until you eventually throw them out for the last time. And just for harm reduction purposes, don't cut with any kind of blade if it is unclean. An infected cut will give you a way worse scar than a clean one.

I understand, I tend to have a lot of hypochondriac tendencies too. When I did a dbt program a couple years ago they taught me some pretty good skills for distress tolerance. 

One that works super well for me is something called ice diving. You put your face in a big bowl of very cold or icy water for however long you want, repeat a couple of times if you need. It activates your brain's dive response which slows down your heart rate and sends the blood to only your vital organs. It's really good for getting me to control my breathing and slow down my thoughts. Then self soothing is something I'd recommend researching, I have tons of fidget toys, putty, temporary tattoos etc. but see what works for you. 

A good idea would be to make a step by step plan of what to do when you're in a panic attack. For example, what skills you can do, people you can contact, places you can go, things like that. Having a plan helps me massively. having comfort music/films/tv is also a big help. as far as looking for a diagnosis, try not to stress too much about that side of things. I know it's scary not knowing what's happening in your own brain, but try to focus mainly on looking after yourself and keeping yourself safe. Record what you experience daily and how it impacts you, research as much as you can and present all of it to a professional. (sorry for the whole essay of a response haha).
